source.title: Visualizing High-Dimensional Trajectories on the Loss-Landscape of ANNs
source.authors: Stefan Horoi; Je-Chun Huang; Bastian Alexander Rieck; Guillaume Lajoie; Guy Wolf; Smita Krishnaswamy

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. Its title differs from the provided TITLE: the paper is titled “Exploring the Geometry and Topology of Neural Network Loss Landscapes.”
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss-landscape features using jump-and-retrain trajectories and topological persistence, then relates them to test loss and generalization. This is a different measure from the claim versions’ specified measures.
record.gate_note: The study reports landscape features associated with test loss and results from classifiers predicting generalization class. It does not test the specific behaviors and measures named in V1–V8. Other sampling-method comparisons are included only where they compare how well sampled features predict generalization.
record.test_reason: The study relates sampled landscape topology to test loss and evaluates its sampling method. It does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization gaps as specified in V7. Its random-label example lacks a matched natural-label experiment and random-label held-out performance needed for V1; the other versions receive no direct comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that jump-and-retrain sampling captures information about generalization and training procedure, and associate better generalization and weight decay with lower topological activity. These are qualitative associations, not a direct test of magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses jump-and-retrain sampling, PHATE visualization, and topological persistence to characterize loss-landscape regions; it does not reproduce the specified methods or measures in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test accuracy varies with data augmentation and weight decay. Total persistence is also described as varying with weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint use of data augmentation and weight decay raises approximate CIFAR-10 test accuracy from 85% to 95%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation and weight decay together improve generalization in the tested wide ResNets.

fits_no_version.finding: Jump-and-retrain features predict generalization class with 39.2% mean accuracy, compared with 30.1% for grid sampling and 31.8% for naive sampling; scrambled features yield 20.7%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jump-and-retrain features contain information about test-loss classes beyond the tested static sampling features.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher total persistence qualitatively accompanies higher test loss, and stronger weight decay accompanies lower topological activity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sampled landscape topology is associated with test loss and regularization in the tested wide ResNets.

record.peer_reviewed: International Symposium on Intelligent Data Analysis
record.problems: The reported persistence-versus-test-loss relationship is presented qualitatively and in a figure without numeric values or a stated statistical test. The classifier results are aggregate means across 11 classifiers.

untested.parts: Matched architectures and training recipes fitting random labels while generalizing on natural labels, and chance-level held-out performance with random labels. Section 4.3 reports approximately zero training loss, but does not supply these matched comparisons.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Held-out performance by batch size under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes. Batch size varies, but no batch-specific performance comparison is reported.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, including small-data and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps, similarly low training-loss comparisons using that measure, and ranking against norm and margin measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply. The landscape and classifier results address related constructs outside the specified versions. Missing results needed to establish V1 or V7 are untested components, rather than reported results omitted from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report held-out accuracy for the randomized-label model or compare its held-out accuracy with chance; does not establish that the same recipes both fit random labels and generalize on natural labels.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold or test-error-versus-width result.
Although batch size varies, the study does not report a large-batch generalization comparison.

Measures topological persistence and trajectory patterns, not magnitude-aware sharpness or weight perturbations; does not compare the version’s named sharpness measure against norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove or retrain on selected memorized examples.

rows.subject: WResNets (108 trained networks; individual model results aggregated)
rows.operation_detail: Reports test accuracy for networks trained with and without data augmentation and weight decay.

conditions.value: data augmentation and weight decay used

rows.baseline: around ∼85% for networks trained without data augmentation and weight decay
rows.value: ∼95% with data augmentation and weight decay
rows.note: Aggregate approximate accuracies; the paper does not give per-network values here.
rows.check: The approximate 85% versus 95% test accuracies describe a joint data-augmentation and weight-decay comparison. No dropout comparison establishes V6.

rows.subject: WResNets (108 trained networks; aggregate classification results)
rows.stage_stated: trained for 200 epochs; jump-and-retrain sampling after training
rows.operation_detail: Uses jump-and-retrain loss and accuracy features to classify networks into five generalization classes based on test loss at optimum.

conditions.value: J&R sampling, retrain loss and accuracy values

rows.note: Mean and standard error across 11 classifiers.
rows.check: This is the study's sampling-method performance, measured by downstream classifiers, rather than an effect named by V1–V8. The reported number is correct.

rows.subject: WResNets (108 trained networks; aggregate classification results)
rows.stage_stated: trained for 200 epochs; scrambled features used in classifier control
rows.operation_detail: Trains classifiers on scrambled versions of the best-performing features as a control.

conditions.value: generalization, weight decay, and data augmentation classification tasks

rows.baseline: Theoretical random: 20.0 for 5-class generalization; 33.3 for weight decay; 50.0 for data augmentation
rows.value: Accuracy is essentially the same as random, according to the text
rows.note: No exact scrambled-feature accuracies are stated.
rows.check: This is a control for the study's downstream classifiers. Contrary to the record, Table 1 gives exact scrambled-feature accuracies: 20.7 ± 1.1% for generalization, 38.9 ± 1.5% for weight decay, and 52.7 ± 1.9% for augmentation.

rows.subject: WResNets (108 trained networks; aggregate association)
rows.stage_stated: trained for 200 epochs; jump-and-retrain sampling after training
rows.operation_detail: Computes total persistence of persistence diagrams for jump-and-retrain samples and relates it to test loss at optimum.
rows.measure: Association between total persistence and test loss at optimum
rows.value: Optima with higher total persistence tend to have higher test loss; optima with lower test loss tend to have lower total persistence
rows.note: The text describes the trend but supplies no numeric values or statistical test for the association.
rows.check: Total persistence versus test loss does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus the training–test gap. Figure 3B specifically reports dimension-zero total persistence; the qualitative trend cannot establish V7.

rows.subject: WResNet16-2
rows.stage_stated: trained to different optima using different training procedures; jump-and-retrain sampling afterward
rows.operation_detail: Compares persistence diagrams and reports qualitative differences in topological activity around optima with different test-set accuracies.

conditions.value: four optima reached by networks with the same initialization but trained in different ways

rows.measure: Qualitative topological activity in sampled manifolds
rows.value: Poorly generalizing optima appear to have more high-persistence points; well-generalizing networks have topological features emerging later in the loss threshold
rows.note: Qualitative comparison; the excerpt does not give the test accuracies for the four optima.
rows.check: Qualitative persistence-diagram differences do not measure V7's sharpness statistic or its ranking against norm and margin measures. The supplied text does not expose the figure's numerical annotations.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
